notes: Ruling slot 18 = UNIP (Kaunda, Zambian Humanism). Coalition slot 19 = the state-socialist Mulungushi wing inside UNIP (catchy). ANC (Nkumbula) in slot 1 as the main opposition; no fitting populated slot for a liberal-conservative party. Slot 0 = banned United Party (Mundia). Slot 4 = ZAPU, the Soviet-backed Zimbabwean movement headquartered in Lusaka, as the main pro-Soviet actor in Zambia. Kapwepwe's Bemba bloc in 20 (populated). UPP (1971) deliberately not added as a period.

0.name: United Party
0.text:
The United Party was founded in 1966 by Nalumino Mundia, a former UNIP minister, and drew its strength from Barotse Province and disaffected Copperbelt workers. After clashes with UNIP militants it was banned in August 1968, and Mundia and his followers carried their support into the African National Congress before the December 1968 election.

The party stood for a business-friendly economy, regional autonomy for Barotseland and good relations with the West and Zambia's southern neighbours. UNIP accused it of receiving money from Rhodesian and South African sources. Its surviving networks among Lozi notables and anti-UNIP townspeople make it a natural home for an authoritarian, Western-leaning alternative.

1.name: African National Congress
1.text:
The African National Congress is Zambia's oldest nationalist party, founded as the Northern Rhodesian ANC and led since 1951 by Harry Mwaanga Nkumbula. It lost the leadership of the independence struggle to UNIP but won 23 seats in the December 1968 election and remains the only legal opposition, strongest in Southern Province among Tonga farmers.

The ANC defends multiparty democracy, private enterprise and the rights of commercial farmers, and opposes the nationalisations of the Mulungushi and Matero reforms. It prefers pragmatic relations with the West and with Rhodesia over confrontation. Its leverage lies in its solid regional base and its role as the rallying point for everyone UNIP has alienated.

2.name: Ubuntungwa
2.text:
Ubuntungwa, the Bemba word for freedom that once rang through the independence rallies, is now the watchword of Lusaka's urban professionals who fear that UNIP is drifting towards a one-party state. Lawyers, journalists, lecturers at the new University of Zambia and church laymen meet in informal circles rather than in any party.

They defend the 1964 constitution, competitive elections, an independent judiciary and a free press, and warn against party-card checks and detention without trial. They favour open trade and Western partners, without abandoning the liberation cause in the south. Their leverage lies in the courts, the press and the educated middle class that the state relies on.

3.name: Zambia Congress of Trade Unions
3.text:
The Zambia Congress of Trade Unions was established by law in 1965 as the single federation of the country's unions, with the powerful Mineworkers' Union of Zambia as its largest affiliate. Its general secretary Wilson Chakulya leads a movement that the government expects to support national development and restrain strikes.

The Congress wants higher wages, Zambianisation of skilled and supervisory jobs in the mines, collective bargaining and social security, while accepting a mixed economy. It looks to the international free trade union movement rather than to Moscow. Its leverage is the Copperbelt: copper earns almost all of Zambia's foreign exchange, and the miners can halt it.

4.name: Zimbabwe African People's Union
4.text:
The Zimbabwe African People's Union is the Rhodesian liberation movement of Joshua Nkomo, banned at home and directed from Lusaka while Nkomo sits in detention. Under James Chikerema and Jason Moyo its external wing runs camps, offices and guerrilla infiltration across the Zambezi with the tolerance of the Zambian government.

ZAPU is armed and trained by the Soviet Union and its allies, and its cadres bring Marxist-Leninist ideas, Soviet scholarships and East bloc contacts into Zambian politics. It wants Zambia as a firm rear base for armed struggle against Rhodesia. Its leverage lies in its weapons, its Soviet patrons and Kaunda's commitment to southern African liberation.

5.name: University of Zambia Students' Union
5.text:
The University of Zambia Students' Union represents the first generation of students at the national university opened in Lusaka in 1966. Influenced by the radical student movements of 1968, by Fanon and by the liberation wars to the south, the students are impatient with the compromises of their elders.

They demand a sharper break with Western mining capital, faster Zambianisation, full support for guerrilla movements and an end to dialogue with Pretoria and Lisbon. They mock official Humanism as too timid. Their leverage lies in demonstrations on Lusaka's streets and in the fact that they are the future elite the state cannot do without.

6.name: Lumpa Church
6.text:
The Lumpa Church is the independent church founded in the 1950s by the prophetess Alice Lenshina in Chinsali district. Its refusal to accept party membership led to bloody fighting with UNIP and security forces in 1964; the church was banned, thousands of followers fled to Katanga and Lenshina remains in detention.

Its followers reject secular political authority, party cards and worldly corruption, and await divine order rather than development plans. They are hostile to the ruling party, to missionary churches and to Western modernity alike. Their leverage is limited to stubborn loyalty in the Northern Province and among exiles, and to the government's fear of renewed millenarian unrest.

7.name: Zambia Police Special Branch
7.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence arm of the Zambia Police, inherited from the colonial administration and steadily Zambianised since independence. It watches opposition politicians, trade unionists, foreign agents and the many liberation movements in Lusaka, and supplies the files used for detentions under the public security regulations.

Its officers favour a strong state, detention without trial and close control of political activity, and see Rhodesian and South African subversion behind every disturbance. They are suspicious of Western embassies and their informants. Their leverage lies in secrecy, in the President's dependence on their reports and in the emergency powers that have remained in force since independence.

8.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Lusaka
8.text:
The Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Lusaka is the small Shia community of Gujarati traders who settled in Northern Rhodesia's line-of-rail towns in the colonial era. Organised around its own mosque and community institutions, it follows the Da'i al-Mutlaq in Bombay and keeps clear of party politics.

The community favours education, orderly commerce and peaceful relations with the government, and is anxious about the 1968 trade licensing reforms that restrict non-citizen traders. It values stable property rights and open trade with East Africa and India. Its leverage lies in retail and wholesale trade along Cairo Road and in the provincial towns.

9.name: Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Lusaka
9.english: Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Lusaka
9.text:
The Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Lusaka is a small community of Twelver Shia families of Indian origin, connected to the Africa Federation of Khoja communities in Dar es Salaam. It follows the senior clerics of Najaf and maintains a mosque and religious school for its members.

In its more devout circles, the authority of the learned jurists is held to stand above secular government, and Western permissiveness and socialist materialism are both rejected. The community has no following among Zambians and no political ambitions in the country. Its influence rests on its religious networks across the Indian Ocean and the business standing of its families.

10.name: Jamaat ya Chipata
10.text:
The Chipata Jamaat stands for the established Muslim congregations of Eastern Province, where Yao migrants from Malawi and Indian traders built the country's oldest mosques. Led by imams trained in the East African coast tradition and backed by merchant trustees, it is the most settled Muslim community in Zambia.

It stands for quiet, apolitical Islam: Quranic schools, family law within the community, loyalty to lawful authority and good relations with Christian neighbours. It distrusts both radical preachers and party militants. Its leverage is limited to a modest religious minority, but it commands respect among traders and in the border region with Malawi.

11.name: Ahl al-Hadith of Lusaka
11.text:
The Ahl al-Hadith of Lusaka is a tiny circle of young Muslims who have returned from religious studies in Medina and Pakistan with a strict, scripture-only Islam. They meet in private homes and in the margins of the capital's mosques, criticising the customs of the established congregations.

They reject both Kaunda's Christian-tinged Humanism and imported socialism, and dream of a worldwide Muslim order under Islamic law. Their pan-Islamism makes them hostile to the West and the communist bloc alike. Their following is minimal, but they have access to Gulf literature and scholarships and to the networks of a revival spreading across the Muslim world.

12.name: Halqa of Kamwala
12.text:
The Kamwala Circle is a study group of Muslim teachers, clerks and traders in Lusaka's Kamwala district who read the works of Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in English and Urdu translation. It works through Islamic classes, welfare for poor Muslims and contacts with visiting preachers from Egypt and Pakistan.

The circle wants an organised Muslim community able to defend its interests, Islamic education alongside state schools and a moral renewal of public life. It rejects atheist socialism and Western materialism but accepts constitutional politics. Its leverage is small but growing among educated Muslim youth on the Copperbelt and along the line of rail.

13.name: Industrial Development Corporation
13.text:
The Industrial Development Corporation is the state holding company that carried out the Mulungushi reforms of 1968, taking majority stakes in breweries, transport, retail and construction firms. Its managing director Andrew Sardanis and his managers now form the core of a new technocratic elite running the commanding heights on the President's behalf.

They favour state capitalism under expert control: parastatals, import substitution, Zambianisation of management and pragmatic deals with foreign partners from East and West. Party ideology matters less to them than efficiency and growth. Their leverage lies in their control of investment, jobs and contracts, and in Kaunda's personal reliance on their advice.

14.name: House of Chiefs
14.text:
The House of Chiefs is the advisory chamber created under the independence constitution in which senior traditional rulers from all provinces debate bills touching on custom, land and chieftaincy. Though it has no veto, it gives the country's chiefs a national platform and a direct line to the government.

The chiefs defend customary land tenure, their role in local justice and the authority of tradition against both party cadres and modernising officials. They are wary of radical socialism and of foreign ideologies of any kind. Their leverage lies in the villages, where most Zambians still live and where a chief's word carries more weight than a party card.

15.name: Anglo American Corporation
15.text:
The Anglo American Corporation of Harry Oppenheimer has dominated the Copperbelt for four decades, together with the American-controlled Roan Selection Trust. Under the Matero reforms announced in August 1969, the government is taking a 51 per cent stake in the mines, but the companies keep management and sales contracts.

The mining houses want generous compensation, security for their contracts, the right to repatriate profits and a free hand in running production. Their outlook is firmly Western, and their headquarters lie in Johannesburg and London. Their leverage remains immense: they still operate the mines that earn nearly all of Zambia's export income and employ its best-paid workers.

16.name: Cairo Road
16.text:
Cairo Road is shorthand for the shopkeepers, wholesalers and small manufacturers of Lusaka's main commercial street and of the Copperbelt towns, many of them of Indian or European origin. The 1968 Mulungushi reforms restricted retail licences outside town centres to citizens, and many now fear for their livelihoods.

They want freedom of trade, an end to licensing discrimination, lower taxes and fewer price controls, and argue that Zambian entrepreneurs need open markets rather than state monopolies. They look to Western economic models. Their leverage lies in their grip on distribution, credit and supply, which the new state corporations cannot quickly replace.

17.name: Luangwa
17.text:
Luangwa stands for the conservationists of the Luangwa valley and Kafue, where park rangers, scientists and pioneers such as Norman Carr have argued since the colonial era that wildlife can be protected by sharing its benefits with local communities. Zambia's national parks, among the largest in Africa, depend on their work.

They want firm action against poaching, protected land in the parks, controlled tourism that brings income to villages and a halt to the reckless clearing of woodland for charcoal and farming. They stand apart from the bloc rivalry. Their leverage lies in tourism revenue, international conservation bodies and the goodwill of chiefs whose lands border the parks.

18.name: United National Independence Party
18.text:
The United National Independence Party, founded in 1959, led Northern Rhodesia to independence as Zambia in 1964 and has governed ever since under President Kenneth Kaunda. It won a large majority in the December 1968 election, though internal rivalries between provincial and ethnic factions strain its unity.

UNIP's doctrine of Humanism blends Christian ethics, African communal values and socialism, and its Mulungushi and Matero reforms bring the economy under state control. It leads the Front Line against white minority rule, belongs to the Non-Aligned Movement and courts both China and the West. Its strength lies in its mass organisation, youth wing and control of the state.

19.name: Mulungushi
19.text:
Mulungushi takes its name from the rock near Kabwe where Kaunda announced the economic reforms of April 1968. It refers to the radical wing of UNIP officials, planners and party intellectuals who see those nationalisations as only the first step towards a fully socialist Zambia.

They want complete state ownership of the mines, banks and foreign trade, cooperatives in the countryside and a party that leads society rather than merely winning elections. They admire Tanzania's Arusha Declaration and Chinese self-reliance, symbolised by the planned Tazara railway. Their leverage lies in the party apparatus and in the President's own leftward turn.

20.name: Abena Kasama
20.text:
The People of Kasama is the Bemba-speaking bloc inside UNIP around Vice-President Simon Kapwepwe, rooted in Northern and Luapula Provinces and the Copperbelt townships. Kapwepwe offered his resignation in August 1969 amid bitter factional quarrels, and his supporters complain that their region has been cheated of its rightful share of power.

They demand faster Zambianisation, the curbing of foreign and Asian businessmen, pride in African culture and dress, and more reward for the provinces that carried the independence struggle. Their populism is hostile to both Western capital and party bureaucrats. Their leverage lies in the votes and miners of the north and in Kapwepwe's personal standing.

21.name: UNIP Youth Brigade
21.text:
The UNIP Youth Brigade is the ruling party's militant youth wing, made up of young urban men who enforce party discipline in markets, bus stations and townships. They check party cards, police political meetings and have clashed violently with supporters of the ANC and the banned United Party.

The Brigade wants an end to opposition parties, compulsory party membership and a nation mobilised under a single leadership. It treats dissent as treachery and foreign residents with suspicion. Its leverage lies in intimidation on the ground, in its numbers in the towns and in the protection it enjoys from party officials who find it useful.

22.name: Zambia Army
22.text:
The Zambia Army grew out of the Northern Rhodesia Regiment and is being rapidly expanded and Zambianised, as British officers on contract are replaced by Zambians. Together with the young Zambia Air Force it guards long borders with Rhodesia, Angola and Mozambique, all controlled by hostile minority regimes.

The officer corps is professional and so far loyal to the civilian government, but it watches military takeovers elsewhere in Africa. It wants modern arms, better pay and a firm defence against Rhodesian and Portuguese raids, and buys equipment from Western and Eastern suppliers alike. Its leverage lies in its weapons and in the frontline security situation.

23.name: Barotse Royal Establishment
23.text:
The Barotse Royal Establishment is the court of the Litunga, the king of the Lozi, at Lealui and Limulunga on the Zambezi floodplain. Litunga Mbikusita Lewanika II, enthroned in 1968, presides over the Kuta council, but the Barotseland Agreement of 1964 that guaranteed the kingdom's autonomy was abrogated by parliament in 1969.

The Establishment demands restoration of the Agreement, control over Barotse land and courts, and respect for the dignity of the Litunga. It distrusts UNIP's centralism and has sympathy for the conservative opposition. Its leverage lies in deep Lozi loyalty to the monarchy and the historic treaties it signed with Britain.
